scores.reason: Shows citation-verification itself is unreliable (3-18% unsupported rate depending on verifier strictness) and validates across models on SciFact — directly moves belief on C2/C3/C5 and on whether reported grounding numbers can be trusted, exactly the premise-stressing work the brief asks for.

Benchmark built for citation-grounded single-paper QA with grounded refusal as a first-class dimension and eight-model comparison — hits C3, C4, and C5 directly, and its finding that citation metrics discriminate where LLM-judge scores compress changes how the authors should measure.

Rigorous biomedical claim-verification evaluation showing retrieval utility is source-dependent and fine-tuned LLMs beat RAG for evidence generation — solid on C2/C5, though it evaluates verification pipelines more than extraction from papers.

CLAIM-BENCH measures claim-evidence extraction from full papers against annotation with six-model comparison and prompting-strategy tradeoffs — the most direct answer to Q1/C1 in the list, plus C3 and C5.

REASONS benchmarks sentence-level citation attribution across 12 domains and quantifies hallucination rates with a RAG mitigation — relevant to C2/C3, though its attribution tasks (title/author matching) are one step removed from claim-evidence linking within papers.

Directly demonstrates a benchmark-construction artifact — NEI label construction silently determines what scores mean in SciFact-style verification and competence does not transfer — hitting C3, C4, and C5 and the brief's explicit ask for construction-inflated accuracy.

Large-scale, doctor-validated quantification of unsupported and contradicted citations (50-90% of responses not fully supported) in a rigorous biomedical setting — the strongest evidence in the list on C2's error-mode question, and it stresses rather than flatters the premise.

Systematic survey of 134 papers and 300 metrics maps the benchmark landscape Q3 asks about and documents that reported numbers are not comparable across evaluation practices — useful background for C3, though it produces no new measurements itself.

Foundational slot: ALCE is the canonical automatic citation-evaluation benchmark that later grounding work builds on; a newcomer skipping it would misread the current papers' evaluation setups and baselines.

Foundational slot: this human-annotated audit established the citation precision/recall framing (51.5%/74.5%) that the newer grounding literature argues with — canonical background a newcomer needs before the rest of the list.
